column4: The section's maysir scene meets this verse's paired questions about gambling and what to spend: it puts taking a chance for a share beside giving from one's means.

The section describes shares drawn by arrows from a slaughtered camel; this verse forbids seeking a portion by divining arrows (الأزلام) and also names carrion. It marks the boundary around that lottery scene.

The section's maysir is listed with divining arrows (الأزلام) among forbidden practices. Its wording to avoid them, فاجتنبوه, shares the ج ن ب root the section notes in 92:17, where the God-fearing are kept away from the Fire.

This continues the prohibition in 5:90 and names gambling's own consequence: Satan seeks hostility and distraction from prayer through it. That gives the section's chance-based pursuit of shares a social and devotional cost.

The verse says its speakers assign a portion of crops and livestock to God and another to their partners. This is a direct livestock-allocation scene, but the section's account locates true ownership with the Lord rather than humanly assigned shares.

Continuing the arbitrary livestock portions in 6:136, this verse describes crops and animals declared inaccessible to all but those the speakers choose, and animals restricted by their claims. Its own detail is who may take from the allotment.

The same allocation passage specifies that what is in some animals' wombs is reserved for males and forbidden to wives, while a dead birth is shared. It supplies a particularly concrete, gendered division of livestock portions.

This completes the livestock passage by condemning the killing of children and prohibiting what God provided. It identifies the cost of fabricated rules over provision, beyond the preceding verses' partition scheme.

After sacrificial camels are slaughtered, this verse directs people to eat from them and feed the needy. It recalls the section's divided camel, while locating its distribution in worship and care rather than a lottery.

This explains the camel offering in 22:36: neither its meat nor blood reaches God; piety does. It separates the material shares in the section's scene from the devotion that gives an offering its value.

The verse stages a drawing of lots (يُلْقُونَ أَقْلَامَهُمْ) to decide who will care for Mary. This parallels the section's lot-drawn assignment, while the outcome is a duty of care rather than a material stake.
Jonah takes part in a draw and is among those who lose; 37:142 completes the consequence by saying the fish swallowed him. The lot here exposes someone to loss, unlike the section's winner's share.

The section's dictionary form الخَلَاق means a portion or share; here inheritance is assigned to men and women as a prescribed share (نَصِيبًا مَفْرُوضًا), a fixed entitlement rather than a chance division.
The section identifies خَلَاق from the خ ل ق root as a share. This verse uses خَلَاق to deny an afterlife share to those who ask only for worldly life, making the portion depend on what they seek.

The section's dictionary form الخَلَاق, from root خ ل ق, means a share. This verse says those who sell their covenant for a small price have no share in the Hereafter, and adds that God will not purify them.

The verse contrasts those seeking the harvest of the Hereafter with those seeking the worldly harvest, for whom it says there is no share in the Hereafter. It makes the section's contrast between a worldly payout and an enduring allotment explicit.

The section's giver parts with his wealth; this verse depicts people feeding the poor, orphan, and captive despite their own love of food. It gives concrete recipients to giving rather than taking a lot-drawn share.

This explains the feeding in 76:8: the givers seek God's face and want neither recompense nor thanks. It closely matches the section's claim that the giver has no favor to repay and gives only seeking his Lord's face.

The section says the man's wealth cannot avail him when he falls; here the condemned speaker says, ما أغنى عني ماليه, “my wealth did not avail me.” The same مال root makes the failed claim of possession explicit.
After the failed wealth claim in 69:28, this verse says the speaker's authority has perished. It extends the section's limit on مال from possessions to worldly power.

The section says مال will not avail its owner; this verse says Abu Lahab's wealth and earnings did not avail him (ما أغنى عنه ماله وما كسب). It gives another explicit reversal of wealth's presumed power.
The verse says disbelievers' wealth and children will not avail them against God and names the Fire as their end. It repeats the section's limit on مال as protection in the Hereafter.

Here the wealth and children of God's opponents will not avail them against Him; the verse places them among the people of the Fire. It specifies the afterlife boundary of the section's property theme.

The verse calls believers to spend from what God has made them successors over (مُسْتَخْلَفِينَ فِيهِ). That directly grounds the section's claim that one's مال is held under God's ownership and should be given.
After condemning stinginess, the verse says the inheritance of the heavens and earth belongs to God. It supports the section's claim that the holder of wealth is not its final owner.

The section's gloss for عِندَهُ describes what is present or near, and it asks who owns what a person has. This verse contrasts what is with people and ends with what is with God, which remains (مَا عِنْدَكُمْ يَنْفَدُ وَمَا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ بَاقٍ).

The section explains the word رَبّ as owner and quotes the dictionary form “Lord of everything.” This verse states of God, وَهُوَ رَبُّ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ, anchoring the section's claim that the allotter and owner is the Lord.

The verse says dominion is given or taken by God, who honors and humbles whom He wills. It locates rank and possession in God's hand, unlike the section's arrow game where a high-value draw wins a share.

The verse says God has favored some over others in provision, then asks whether recipients would share it equally with those under their authority. It describes unequal shares as provision from God, not winnings from an arrow draw.

The verse explicitly says, نَحْنُ قَسَمْنَا بَيْنَهُم مَّعِيشَتَهُمْ, “We divided their livelihood among them,” and mentions differing degrees. It locates material allotment with God rather than chance.

This verse says that if God expanded provision without limit people would overreach, so He sends it down by a measure as He wills. It gives the section's measured shares a divine limit rather than a lottery's contingency.
The section links the root خ ل ق in 92:3 to an allotted share; this verse says, إِنَّا كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقْنَاهُ بِقَدَرٍ, joining creation to measure.

The section's root خ ل ق carries the dictionary sense of a measured portion. This verse says God created everything and measured it precisely (فَقَدَّرَهُ تَقْدِيرًا), a direct formulation of creation under measure.

The section connects the root ع ل و to the highest arrow, al-Muʿallā, and to the Lord named al-Aʿlā. This verse calls Him the Most High (الْأَعْلَى), grounding that elevation in the Lord rather than the arrow's rank.
The section links creation's خ ل ق root to an allotted share. This adjacent verse says God created and proportioned (خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ), joining creation to ordered form.

The next verse says God measured and guided (قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ). It completes the creation-and-order sequence of 87:2 and echoes the section's measured share and its claim that guidance belongs to God.

The verse tells each person to spend according to the provision given to him and promises ease after hardship (يُسْرًا). It connects the section's ease root ي س ر with spending measured by one's means, rather than a chance draw.

This verse commands spending from what God has provided and calls protection from one's own stinginess success. It spells out the section's giving-versus-withholding distinction as a choice about God's provision.

The section describes giving wealth to purify oneself; this verse says the one who purifies the soul succeeds. It supplies a direct Quranic statement of the purification the section associates with giving.
The next verse gives the reverse of 91:9: the one who corrupts the soul fails. It sharpens the section's contrast between giving that purifies and withholding.
The section asks who owns one's share and cites the question, “Does a human have whatever he desires?” This verse challenges desire as a claim to possession.
The answer to 53:24 is that the Hereafter and the first life belong to God (فَلِلَّهِ الْآخِرَةُ وَالْأُولَىٰ). It directly grounds the section's claim that first and last are God's.

The section cites this verse's wording that praise belongs to God in the first and the Hereafter. It applies the same temporal pair to praise and judgment, alongside the section's claim about God's ownership of both.
The verse says the Hereafter will be better for the Prophet than the first life. It repeats the section's first/last pair while adding a particular promise of the latter's superiority.

This verse tells Qarun to seek the Hereafter through what God has given him, while not neglecting his share of this world. It connects property to seeking the lasting good rather than treating possession as final.
The verse says righteousness is not reached until one spends from what one loves. It makes the section's act of giving wealth a specific test of what is valued.
The verse warns that charity is undone by reminders of one's favor or by injury. That sets a boundary around the section's giver who is owed no recompense and acts without a debt to collect.
This verse distinguishes money given for increase from alms given seeking God's face. It clarifies the section's contrast between a material stake in maysir and giving for the Lord's pleasure.
The verse condemns those who hoard gold and silver rather than spend it in God's way. It gives the section's withholding of مال a concrete form with a stated consequence.
This continues the hoarding warning of 9:34: the hoarded metal becomes a punishment, and the verse identifies it as what they stored for themselves. It shows stored wealth turning against its holder.
The verse depicts a man treating expanded provision as proof that his Lord honored him. It parallels the section's property-and-rank image, then its context challenges that reading.

The man in this verse treats restricted provision as humiliation; the wording says God measured his provision (قَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ). It makes an allotted share concrete, while the next ayah rejects the man's interpretation.
The “No!” here corrects the claim in 89:15–16: the problem is failure to honor the orphan. It supports the section's account of moral difference as giving, not the amount of wealth received.
The same correction says people do not urge one another to feed the poor. It supplies a specific failure to give, echoing the section's distinction between generosity and withholding.
The verse describes devouring inheritance wholesale. It connects the section's property and apportioned shares to what happens when people consume others' portions instead of giving.
The verse condemns excessive love of wealth. It names the inward attachment that stands against the section's giver, who parts with property for God's face.
The verse calls wealth and children adornments of worldly life, while enduring good deeds are better. It adds what lasts to the section's claim that possession cannot secure the Hereafter.
The verse says that on the Day wealth and children will not avail anyone. This is a direct afterlife counterpart to the section's claim that a man's مال cannot help him when he falls.
The exception in the next verse is whoever comes to God with a sound heart. It completes the limit on wealth in 26:88 with an inward condition, alongside the section's purifying gift.

The verse says wealth and children do not bring people near to God; faith and righteous action do. It distinguishes possession from the standing the section assigns to generosity and seeking the Lord's face.
This verse commands full measure and just weighing in trade. It offers an economic counterpart to the section's measured shares: a just quantity rather than a portion fixed by a lottery.
The surah opens by condemning those who give short measure. It gives a concrete boundary for the section's share theme: portions in exchange must not be secretly reduced.
This identifies the short-measure traders as people who demand their full measure from others. It adds the one-sided taking that makes their division unjust.
The same traders reduce what they measure or weigh for others. It completes the image of unjust portions in 83:1–2 and contrasts with a genuinely measured share.
The verse says whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. It makes the section's ease-by-giving claim a measured moral outcome rather than a chance payout.
The paired verse says whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it. It completes the measured return of 99:7 and sets a moral boundary around the section's distribution-by-chance scene.
The verse describes those whose scales are heavy, making deeds the measure of outcome. It contrasts the section's arrow-drawn share with a weighed judgment.
The person with heavy scales is promised a pleasant life. This gives the measured outcome in 101:6 its result, echoing the section's ease for the giver.
The verse turns to the person whose scales are light. It makes the section's contrary outcome for withholding a matter of measured deeds rather than a chance draw.
This names the light-weighed person's destination as the abyss, completing 101:8. It gives the consequence of the opposite measured outcome, a boundary to the section's ease.

The section's dictionary sense for root خ ل ق includes measuring leather before cutting. This verse commands David to measure the links of his armor carefully; the craft is a specific parallel in fitting measured material, though it concerns armor rather than leather.
